newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy metalworkers hold big strikes for contracts.
newsitem.headline: Italy metalworkers hold big strikes for contracts.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of people marched through Italian cities on Friday in a one-day national strike by some 1.5 million engineering and metalworkers seeking pay increases.
The biggest demonstrations were in Milan and Turin. Some 50,000 workers marched in each of the northern industrial cities and took part in rallies addressed by union leaders.
The strikers, many of whom carried banners and flags, included workers from factories of car giant Fiat in Turin and from computer maker Olivetti in Ivrea.
Smaller demonstrations took place in cities as far south as Naples, where 20,000 people demonstrated, and the Sicilian capital Palermo.
The eight-hour stoppage, which mainly affected industrial production line workers, was the first nationwide strike in the sector over pay since 1990.
Negotiations for a renewal of contracts between employers and the FIM, FIOM and UILM unions broke down earlier this month.

Unions have demanded an overall wage rise of 10.1 percent over the next two years, while employers' group Federmeccanica has offered increases of between seven and nine percent -- in line with contracts already renewed in other Italian sectors.
The strike took place as Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government was poised to approve a deficit-cutting budget in a dash to join a European single currency.
A number of demonstrators shouted slogans accusing the government of sacrificing workers rights' on the altar of European Union.
Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the hard left Communist Refoundation party, joined the march in Milan.
Prodi's government, which includes the former communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), relies on support from Bertinotti's small party in the lower house of parliament.
"Today's strike...is an important step for workers, for the left and for Italy. It shows that the important question of salaries is still an open one in our country," Bertinotti said.
Bertinotti has become a virtual folk hero among the Italian working class for insisting that budget cuts do not overly affect pensions and social security benefits.
The strike was a blow to Prodi's government, which has been trying to convince unions to accept moderate wage increases to help in the fight against inflation.

The unions had demanded that their members should be compensated in full for a 4.1 percent loss of purchasing power during the old contract period of June 1994-June 1996, when inflation was higher than expected.

Industrialists have argued that the economic downturn prevents a more generous pay claim and say rising labour costs, coupled with recent rises in the value of the lira, will wipe out past competitive gains.
In other industrial action, a union representing air traffic controllers held a four-hour strike and the national airline Alitalia said its services were severely disrupted.
